overview.title: 📖 Overview: Forgotten Pots, Returned Pots, and a New Kind of Fire
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 38a–38b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמְבַשֵּׁל בְּשַׁבָּת, בְּשׁוֹגֵג — יֹאכַל, בְּמֵזִיד — לֹא יֹאכַל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with the question left hanging at the end of the previous one: if a pot was forgotten on the stove and cooked through on Shabbat, may its food be eaten? The Gemara works through two readings of a terse ruling, a later penalty enacted against people who falsely claimed to have 'forgotten,' and a story about Rabbi Yosei's differing rulings on hot water versus shriveled eggs. It then asks whether Beit Hillel's permission to 'return' a pot applies even during Shabbat itself, before a new mishna introduces two more heat sources — the oven (tanur) and the intermediate kupach — each with its own rules.

slides.title: 🍲 The Forgotten Pot: Two Ways to Read 'It Is No Different'
slides.subtitle: A sage's terse ruling sparks a fundamental debate

nodes.content: ❓ One who cooks on Shabbat: unwitting may eat, intentional may not — 'and it is no different.' No different from what?

columns.label: Rabba & Rav Yosef (lenient)
columns.content: Only actively cooking is judged by intent. One who merely forgot a pot performed no act at all — even if he left it intentionally, he may still eat

columns.label: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak (strict)
columns.content: A cook has no reason to deceive, so unwitting cooking is always fine. But a 'forgetter' might be lying — even genuine forgetting becomes forbidden

nodes.content: 🤔 A baraita is cited that fits neither view cleanly — the Gemara leaves the difficulty standing: קַשְׁיָא

slides.title: 🔥 Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda on the Forgotten Pot
slides.subtitle: The baraita distinguishes by how far the food had already cooked
rows: Unwitting: may eat; intentional: may not
May eat either way (unwitting or intentional)
Permitted — such water only shrivels and deteriorates, so no one would stoke the coals
May eat either way (unwitting or intentional)
Forbidden — such food shrivels and improves (e.g. cabbage, beans, minced meat), so stoking is a real concern

slides.title: 🥚 Rabbi Yosei's Visit to Tzippori
slides.subtitle: Hot water permitted, shriveled eggs forbidden — and why
slides.hebrewSource: בֵּיצִים מְצוּמָּקוֹת שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּהוּ עַל גַּבֵּי כִּירָה, וְאָסַר לָהֶן
slides.label: The incident:
slides.text: When Rabbi Yosei visited Tzippori, he found hot water left on the stove and did not forbid it, but he found eggs shriveled from overcooking left on the stove — and he forbade them. The Gemara initially wonders if he was ruling out eating them that Shabbat, but concludes he was only warning against doing so the following Shabbat. The reason for the distinction: shriveled eggs actually improve the longer they cook, as Rav Chama bar Chanina recalled eating many delicious shriveled eggs, the size of crab apples, as a guest of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — so leaving eggs risks someone stoking the coals for a better result.

slides.title: 🔄 Does 'Even Return' Include Returning on Shabbat Itself?
slides.subtitle: Beit Hillel's leniency tested against real practice

lines.speaker: Rav Sheshet
lines.text: When the mishna says Beit Hillel 'even permit returning' a pot, that includes returning it during Shabbat itself — not only while it is still Friday.

lines.speaker: Rav Oshaya
lines.text: Once we stood before Rabbi Chiyya the Great on Shabbat, carried a kettle of hot water up a floor, poured him a cup, and returned it to its place — and he said nothing to us.

lines.speaker: R. Tadai
lines.text: But this is only permitted while the pot is still in one's hand; once set down on the ground, returning it is forbidden.

lines.speaker: R. Chiyya/R. Yochanan
lines.text: Not so — even a pot already placed on the ground may still be returned to the stove.

callout.label: Left unresolved:
callout.text: Later amora'im further debate whether original intent to return makes the difference, and dilemmas about hanging a pot on a stick or transferring between urns are left as teiku, unresolved.

slides.title: 🔥 New Mishna: Stove, Oven, and the In-Between Kupach
slides.subtitle: Three heat sources, three different levels of restriction

boxes.title: Stove (Keirah)
items: Placing food on top is permitted once swept/ashed

boxes.title: Kupach (small stove)
items: Lit with straw/rakings: treated like a stove — leaning permitted, placing on top forbidden
Lit with pomace/wood: treated like an oven — even leaning is forbidden
Rav Ashi: heat greater than a stove's, less than an oven's

boxes.title: Oven (Tanur)
items: Nothing may be placed inside or on top, even when lit with quick-burning straw
Even leaning against it is forbidden
The most intense heat of the three

callout.label: Sizing rule:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: a kupach holds space for one pot; a stove holds space for two — which is also why, for ritual purity, a broken stove split lengthwise stays pure but split widthwise remains two functioning (impure) stoves, while a broken kupach is always pure either way.

summary.principle: Whether accidentally-cooked or deliberately-returned food may be eaten or moved on Shabbat depends on intent, on how fully the food was already cooked, and on which heat source — stove, kupach, or oven — is involved, each carrying its own graduated set of restrictions.

flowSteps.content: 🍲 Forgotten pot debate: Rabba/Rav Yosef judge only active cooking by intent; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak penalizes even forgetting
🔥 Rabbi Meir permits fully-cooked food regardless of intent; Rabbi Yehuda splits by shrivel-improves vs. shrivel-deteriorates
🥚 Rabbi Yosei forbids shriveled eggs (which improve) but not hot water (which does not)

columns.content: 🔄 Rav Sheshet: Beit Hillel's 'even return' applies even during Shabbat itself, per Rav Oshaya's story
🔥 New mishna: stove, kupach, and oven form a graduated scale of restriction

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the underlying worry is always the same — that permitting one leniency will tempt someone to stoke the coals

quiz.q: How do Rabba and Rav Yosef read the ruling 'it is no different' regarding one who forgot a pot on the stove?
o: Forgetting is always forbidden, just like intentional cooking
Since forgetting involves no active deed, one may eat the food even if the pot was left intentionally
The ruling applies only to eggs
Forgetting is punished more severely than intentional cooking
quiz.e: Rabba and Rav Yosef distinguish actively cooking (judged by intent) from merely forgetting a pot (no act performed, so permitted even if left on purpose).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda's view in the baraita, why is fully-heated hot water permitted to eat, while fully-cooked food is not?
o: Water is never considered 'cooked'
Water shrivels and deteriorates with more heat, so there is no temptation to stoke the coals; food like cabbage or beans improves, creating that temptation
Food is always more expensive than water
There is no such distinction in Rabbi Yehuda's view
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda's rule hinges on shrivel-and-improve versus shrivel-and-deteriorate: food that would benefit from more heat is forbidden due to the risk of stoking coals.

quiz.q: Why did Rabbi Yosei forbid the shriveled eggs left on the stove at Tzippori but not the hot water?
o: Eggs are always forbidden on Shabbat
Shriveled eggs actually improve with more cooking, creating concern that someone would stoke the coals
The water had already cooled down
Eggs cannot be reheated according to Torah law
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that shriveled eggs shrivel-and-improve (as shown by Rav Chama bar Chanina's story of enjoying such eggs as a guest), unlike hot water.

quiz.q: What does Rav Oshaya's story about carrying a kettle to Rabbi Chiyya the Great demonstrate?
o: That returning a pot is forbidden under all circumstances
That Beit Hillel's 'even return' leniency applies even to returning a pot during Shabbat itself, not only beforehand
That kettles may never be moved on Shabbat
That only priests may pour hot water on Shabbat
quiz.e: Rav Oshaya cites this incident to support Rav Sheshet's view that the mishna's permission to return a pot applies even when done on Shabbat itself.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is the status of a kupach lit with pomace or wood?
o: It is treated like a stove and food may be placed on top
It is treated like an oven, so even leaning a pot against it is forbidden
It has no restrictions at all
It is only used for baking bread, never for pots
quiz.e: A kupach lit with pomace or wood takes on the stricter status of an oven, where even leaning a pot against it is prohibited.
